verses.166:
> Yet ˹if you are denied, O Prophet,˺ Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you—He has sent it with His knowledge. The angels too bear witness. And Allah ˹alone˺ is sufficient as a Witness

**God Bears Witness**
The verse answers the men who deny the message by naming a witness who cannot be doubted: God bears witness to what He sent down to the Prophet, and He sent it with His knowledge, and the angels also bear witness, and God is enough as a witness. The verse follows the account of why the messengers were sent (4:165) and the list of messengers who were named and unnamed (4:164).

**What the Witness Means Here**
The men the sūrah has been answering did not ask for proof in the ordinary sense; they asked for an arrangement that suited them, and the Book's answer is that the message has a witness whose testimony settles the matter. The sūrah has said the same at several points in this chapter: it told the Prophet that God is enough as a guardian and a helper (4:45 says that God knows the community's enemies best and that He is enough as a protector), it described the knowledge that was given to the Prophet so that he could answer the arguments brought to him (4:105 sets the standard of judgment and 4:113 names what he was taught), and it gave the community the rule that reports must be checked before they are acted on (4:83 states it). The verse in front of the reader puts the whole question of who has the last word in one sentence.

**The Angels as Witnesses**
The verse names the angels beside God, which the Book does elsewhere when it describes the day of account: the sūrah says that every community will be brought with a witness and the Prophet will be brought as a witness over his own (4:41 describes that scene), and it says that the angels were present when the souls of the men who wronged themselves were taken (4:97 reports their words). The same sūrah names the angels in its call to believe in them, so that faith covers the messengers, the books, the angels, and the last day (the list appears in the chapter's own call to believe). The verse in front of the reader places the heavenly witness beside the human denial: the ones who keep the record are named, and the record is the thing the men in the passage have been ignoring all along.

**What the Passage Has Built**
The verses before this one recited a long history of men who argued with messengers: the demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153), the broken covenant (4:155), the slander against Mary (4:156), the claim about the crucifixion (4:157), the forbidden foods (4:160), and the interest they took (4:161). The chapter answered that history with the witness it names here, and then it turned to the men in the same communities who believed and did right (4:162 gives the list). The verse in front of the reader is the point where the argument stops being about evidence and becomes about what a person does with the news.

**The Rest of the Chapter**
The verses after this one describe the men who rejected the message and held others back from the road (4:167 states the charge), the men who wronged themselves and will be led to no path but the fire (4:168) and (4:169 give the two verses), and then the direct address to all humanity that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it) and the warning to the People of the Book against extremes in their faith (4:171 gives the warning). The sūrah has kept the same frame around the whole section: it told the community to be mindful of God and to keep its agreements, and it said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God with the knowledge that surrounds it (4:126 states both), that no deed escapes the account (4:40 sets the scale), and that the private talk which urges good earns a reward (4:114). It also described the men whose plans are written down at night (4:108) and the men who look for honour in the wrong company (4:139), and it named the men who practiced a prayer for an audience (4:142), the men who belonged to neither side (4:143) and the men who took the other side as allies (4:144). The verse in front of the reader answers every one of those positions with a single fact: what was sent down was sent with knowledge, and the One who sent it is watching the answer each person gives. The sūrah had already named the men who keep their agreements and stand for justice (4:135 sets the standard) and the men who hand back what was entrusted to them (4:58), and it named the messengers who came with news and warning so that no one would have an argument left (4:165). The sūrah has promised the gardens to the men who believe and do good work (4:122) and has dealt with the question the community asked about women and orphans (4:127). It has recorded the instruction to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book (4:131), has said that God takes care of every affair (4:132), and has placed both rewards with Him (4:134). It has named the pick-and-choose position on the messengers (4:150), has recorded that every one of the People of the Book will believe in Jesus before his death (4:159), and has listed the prophets who carried the message before the Prophet (4:163). It has also described the men who went back to the fight whenever they could (4:91) and has told the community to verify what it strikes before it strikes (4:94).

---## Verse 4:167
> Those who disbelieve and hinder ˹others˺ from the Way of Allah have certainly strayed far away

**Rejecting the Message and Blocking Others**
The verse describes people who reject the message and then stand in other people's road, turning them away from the way of God. It says of them that they have gone far astray. The verse follows the witness named just before it (4:166 names the witness), and it names the second half of the offence. It is not only a refusal to walk the road, but a blocking of the road for everyone else.

**The Two Sides of the Offence**
The Book treats a person who misleads others as carrying something extra, and this chapter makes the point more than once. It says that a man who blames an innocent neighbour for his own fault carries a double load (4:112 describes that man). It says that a man who earns a fault and then throws it onto someone else carries both the slander and the plain sin (4:111 states it). This verse names the same doubling in another setting. Those who hold others back from God's road do harm twice: to themselves and to the people who would have listened to them.

The sūrah has already shown what that looks like inside a community. It describes men who take the other side as allies because it seemed safer (4:139 describes the practice), men who sit with those who mock God's verses (4:140 covers that instruction), men whose loyalty is flexible so that they belong to neither side (4:143 states it), and men who held back when the order to march came and then wanted a share of the gains (4:72 names them).

**Where the Chapter Names This Wrong Elsewhere**
The sūrah charges the same wrong to the earlier community in the passage just before. The verse that forbade certain foods gave the reason that they turned many people away from God's road (4:160 states the reason), and the verse before it named the interest they took and the property they devoured (4:161 gives both charges). It charges the same to the community standing in front of it when it describes men who wanted a tyrant's court to judge between them (4:60 states the case) and men who turned away when they were called to the Book (4:61 names them). This verse sums up the whole attitude: a man who does not want the road for himself and does not want it for anybody else.

**The Verdict Stated**
The verse says that such people have gone far astray. The same language has been used for other wrong turns in this chapter. It was used of the men who reached the wrong destination through a chain of errors (4:116 names the wrong that cannot be forgiven), of the men who had the road made clear and then walked away (4:115 gives that case), and of the men who wanted the reward without the conduct (4:123 refuses the wish). The chapter also warns that such positions do not stay still. It says that God left the men who chose their own direction to it (4:115 again), and it says that a man who is left to wander will not find a way (4:143 states the rule).

**What the Chapter Keeps Beside This Warning**
Much stands beside this warning in the verses around it. The men who are grounded in knowledge and believe in what was sent to the Prophet and before him are given their wage (4:162 lists them). Those who accept all of the messengers are promised their reward (4:152 states it). Those who turn back and put things right are counted with the believers (4:146 names the four conditions). And the people excused from the journey are described with mercy, since God names the helpless among men, women and children (4:98 names them and 4:99 states their case).

The sūrah also reminds its readers what the whole Book is for. God's will in it is to make matters clear (4:26 states it). God owns the heavens and the earth and knows everything (4:126 states it). Both rewards are with Him (4:134 says it). And the people who were given the Book before were told the same thing the community is told (4:131 records the command). The chapter names the men among them who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and in what was sent before (4:162 appears again), and it says that the road of the people who follow the light is named near the close of the chapter (4:175 mentions it).

**Where the Passage Turns Next**
The two verses that follow state what happens to the people described here. They will not be forgiven, and they will not be guided to any path except the road of the fire (4:168 and 4:169 give the two verses). Then the chapter turns to all humanity with the news that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it) and to the People of the Book with a warning against extremes (4:171 gives it).

The sūrah names the people who did otherwise at every point where it names the people who did wrong. It names those who keep the prayer and pay the alms (4:162 lists them), those who migrate and find room in the earth (4:100 gives the promise), those who strive in God's way with their wealth and their lives (4:95 names the rank given them), and those who ask God only for what is good (4:134 says that both rewards are with Him). The verse says what happens when a person decides that his refusal has to be everybody's refusal.

**The Chapter's Other Threads**
Other threads run beside this one. The sūrah tells the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 gives the instruction). It handles the couple whose marriage had gone cold (4:128 describes them) and the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129 commands it). It gives the community the list of what belief covers (4:136 gives the list). It names the prophets who carried the message (4:163 lists them) and the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164 names them). And it states the purpose of the whole sending, which is that nobody would have an argument left (4:165 gives that purpose).
verses.168:
> Those who disbelieve and wrong themselves—surely Allah will neither forgive them nor guide them to any path

**Not Forgiven and Not Guided**
The verse says that the men who reject the message and wrong themselves will not be forgiven and will not be guided to any path. The verse follows the account of the men who block others from the road of God (4:167) and it states the consequence in two parts: no forgiveness, and no road.

**What the Verse Is Not Saying**
The Book does not say that a man who has done wrong cannot come back, and the whole chapter contradicts that reading. The sūrah opened the door of asking forgiveness to the man who does wrong and then turns to God (4:110 states it), described the four conditions under which the men whose belief was a show could be counted with the believers (4:146 lists them), and asked what God would gain from punishing anyone who is grateful and believing (4:147 gives the question). The verse in front of the reader is about men who did not ask, did not turn, and did not stop holding others back: the wrong they did to themselves is the thing that kept them where they were.

**The Wrong Done to Oneself**
The Book describes sin as a wrong done to the person who commits it, and the sūrah has used the phrase before: it named the men who were taken in death while they had wronged themselves and who called themselves weak (4:97 reports it and follows with the men, women and children who were genuinely helpless at 4:99). It told the community that whoever earns a fault has earned it against himself (4:111 states it), and it described the man who does a wrong or a sin and then throws the blame on an innocent person as carrying the slander and the plain sin (4:112 gives that picture). The verse in front of the reader names the same fact: the men who reject the message are not harming God by it, and the chapter has said as much when it said that a people can be removed and others brought in their place (4:133 states it).

**The Road That Is Withheld**
The verse says that such men will not be guided to any path, and the sūrah has shown what guidance means in the chapter's own terms: it named the men who were guided for their own good (4:26 speaks of God's will to make things clear and to guide), it said that God does not wrong a soul by the weight of an atom (4:40 sets the scale), and it named the men whose hearts are kept from the truth because of what they chose (the sūrah's account of the earlier community says that God sealed their hearts as a consequence). The verse in front of the reader states the same principle with two negations. The men in the passage had the message in front of them, the witness named (4:166 states that God bears witness to what was sent down), and their own history to read (4:157 records the claim about the crucifixion and the correction that followed).

**What the Chapter Has Placed Opposite**
The sūrah has set the other road beside this one in the verses immediately around it: the men and women who believe in God and the last day and do good work are given their wage (4:162 lists them), the men who accept all of the messengers are promised their reward (4:152 states it), the men who turn back and mend what they broke are counted with the believers (4:146 names the conditions), and the men who follow the light sent down with the Prophet are named at the close of the chapter (4:175 states their road). The chapter keeps the same two columns from its early pages: the men who believe and do good work (4:122 names the gardens) against the men who look for honour in the wrong company (4:139 states the answer), and the men who ask forgiveness (4:110 opens the door) against the men who keep the road closed to others (4:167 gives the charge). The verse in front of the reader belongs to the second column, and the verses after it turn to the widest address in the chapter: the call to all humanity that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170 states it). The sūrah has described the knowledge given to the Prophet for the arguments brought to him (4:113) and has warned the man who walks away from the road once it has been made clear (4:115). It has described the men who went back and forth between belief and denial (4:137), has named the interest the earlier community took (4:161), and has named the helpless who are excused because they had no way out (4:99).

---## Verse 4:169

> except that of Hell, to stay there for ever and ever. And that is easy for Allah

**The Road of the Fire**
The verse states what the men described in the verses before it are guided to: the road of hell, where they will remain, and it says that this is easy for God. The verse follows the statement that such men will not be forgiven or guided (4:168) and it completes the sentence with the destination.

**What the Verse Names**
The Book describes the two destinations as two roads and it places the journey of each person on one of them. This chapter has already named both roads in its own way: it named the men who follow the light that has been sent down with the Prophet as the successful ones (4:175 states their road), the men who obey God and the Messenger as the company of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous (4:69 names the company), and the men who are taken in death while they have wronged themselves as the men whose dwelling is hell (4:97 reports their state). The verse in front of the reader is the plain statement of the other end of the road, and it comes at the close of the passage on the men who kept others off the way of God.

**Remaining There**
The verse says that the men on this road will remain in it, and the Book uses the same word for the reward of the men who did good when it describes the gardens that the believers will be given (the sūrah states the same permanence for the reward of the men and women who believe and do good work at 4:122). The verse's point is not the length of the punishment but the finality of the choice: the men in the passage had the message, the warnings, the reading of their own history, and the door that stays open in this life (4:146 names the conditions and 4:110 opens the door of asking). The sūrah has said the same about the men whose hearts were sealed by their own conduct (4:155 states the consequence for the earlier community) and about the men who were left to the direction they chose (4:115 gives that case).

**Ease for God**
The verse closes by saying that this is easy for God, the same phrase the sūrah has used elsewhere for what God does without trouble: it said that God is able to remove a people and bring others in their place (4:133 states it), it promised the couple who separate that God will enrich each of them from His abundance (4:130 states the promise), it said that the wrong that is not forgiven will not be forgiven (4:116 gives the rule), and it named the fire as the destination for the men who consume the property of orphans and for the men who kill a believer on purpose (4:10) and (4:93 name the two). The verse in front of the reader closes a passage that has run from the slander against Mary to the men who block the road with a reminder that the matter is not hard for the one who keeps the account.

**Where the Chapter Goes From Here**
The verse after this one turns to all humanity: the Messenger has come with the truth, so believe for your own good, and if you reject, everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, who knows all things and is wise (4:170 states all of it). The chapter then addresses the People of the Book directly, warning them against extremes in their faith and telling them to say nothing about God but the truth (4:171 gives the warning), and it names the Messiah as a messenger of God, a word placed in Mary, and a spirit from Him. The sūrah closes with the rules for the man who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 handles the last case), and it has kept the reader's attention on the two roads all the way through: it named the men who ask forgiveness after doing wrong (4:110), the men who turn back and hold fast to God (4:146), the men whose faith was a show (4:142), the men who waited to see who won (4:141), the men who were taken while they wronged themselves (4:97), and the men among the People of the Book who believed and did right and are given their wage (4:162). The verse in front of the reader says where one of those two roads ends, and the verse after it invites every reader to take the other one. The sūrah has named the home of the men who followed what they were shown (4:121) and the gardens promised to the men who believe and do good work (4:122), has placed both rewards with God (4:134), and has named the place reserved for the men whose belief was a show (4:145). It has passed its verdict on the men who wanted a middle way (4:151), has described the demand for a written revelation from the sky (4:153), and has named the interest the earlier community took (4:161). The verses around this one name the men who block others from the road (4:167), the men who are left where they are (4:168 and 4:169), and the men who guard what they were given (4:172). The sūrah has also said that God's will is to make matters clear (4:26), has warned the community about the marriage that is treated lightly (4:30), and has named the helpless who are excused (4:99). The verse before this one states the same destination in its own words (4:169).

---## Verse 4:170

> O humanity! The Messenger has certainly come to you with the truth from your Lord, so believe for your own good. But if you disbelieve, then ˹know that˺ to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise

**The Address to All Humanity**
The verse turns from the argument with the People of the Book and speaks to everybody: the Messenger has come with the truth from your Lord, so believe, because that is better for you; and if you reject, then everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, who knows all things and is wise. The verse follows the statement of the two roads (4:168) and (4:169) and it opens the chapter's final address.

**Why the Address Is Universal**
The Book widens the frame because the argument of the preceding passage was never only about one community. The chapter opened by addressing all people through the One who created them from a single soul and made families and kinship from it (4:1 states it), and it has dealt with believers, doubters, hypocrites and the holders of earlier Books all the way through. The verse in front of the reader says that the invitation is addressed to everyone, and it gives the reason in two parts: the message brings the truth, and accepting it is good for the person who accepts it. The sūrah has made the same point when it described the reward as a wage rather than a favour (4:100 gives the promise to the man who migrates, and 4:40 sets the scale of every deed).

**Believe for Your Own Good**
The verse's phrase about believing for one's own good is the same point the sūrah made when it asked what God would gain from punishing a grateful believer (4:147 gives the question). The Book says plainly in other passages that a person's faith does not add to God and his refusal does not take from Him, and the chapter has stated the ownership that stands behind it: everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and His knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states both), and He can replace one people with another (4:133 states it). The verse in front of the reader tells the reader that the decision is his, and it tells him whose interest is at stake in it.

**The Names at the End**
The verse closes with the knowing and the wise, the two names the chapter has used at the moments when the argument settles: it named them when it said that God raised the Messiah to Himself (4:158 states it), it named God as knowing what is in the hearts of the men whose words changed at night (4:63 gives the knowledge), and it named the men who were given knowledge and faith as the ones whose understanding is complete (4:162 lists them). The verse in front of the reader puts the two names at the end of a universal invitation: the One who knows everything is inviting people to what benefits them, and there is no hidden reason behind it.

**What the Chapter Has Built Toward This Address, and What Follows**
The verses before this one have carried the whole case: the witness who cannot be doubted (4:166 says that God bears witness to what was sent down), the men who block the road (4:167 names the charge), the men who are not guided because they choose it (4:168 states it), and the road where their choice ends (4:169 names it). Before them came the list of messengers (4:163), the purpose of the sending (4:165), the knowledge given to the Prophet (4:105 states the charge to judge and 4:113 names what he was taught), the charges against the earlier community (4:161 names the interest they took), and the men in that community who believed and did right (4:162 lists them). The chapter had also given the community its own duties: verify what you strike (4:94), return what is entrusted (4:58), keep your agreements (4:33), stand for justice even against your own family (4:135), and remember God in every position (4:103). The verse after this one addresses the People of the Book and warns them against extremes (4:171 gives the warning), and the chapter closes with the rules for the man who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176), naming the road of the men who follow the light (4:175). The sūrah has also kept the door of mercy in view throughout: the men who ask forgiveness after doing wrong (4:110), the men who turn back and mend (4:146), the men and women who do good work with faith (4:124), the helpless who are excused (4:99), and the men who migrate and are given room in the earth (4:100). The verse in front of the reader is the widest of the chapter's invitations, and it comes at the end of the longest of its arguments. The sūrah has said that every sin falls on the man who earns it (4:111), has promised the gardens to the men who believe and do good work (4:122), and has promised the couple who separate that God will enrich them (4:130). It has recorded the instruction to be mindful of God given to the earlier holders of the Book and to the community (4:131), has given the list of what belief covers (4:136), has named the pick-and-choose position (4:150), and has named the reward of the men who accept all of the messengers (4:152). It has named the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164) and has said that no deed escapes the exact account (4:40).

---## Verse 4:171

> O People of the Book! Do not go to extremes regarding your faith; say nothing about Allah except the truth. The Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, was no more than a messenger of Allah and the fulfilment of His Word through Mary and a spirit ˹created by a command˺ from Him. So believe in Allah and His messengers and do not say, “Trinity.” Stop!—for your own good. Allah is only One God. Glory be to Him! He is far above having a son! To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And Allah is sufficient as a Trustee of Affairs

**Do Not Go to Extremes**
The verse addresses the People of the Book and warns them against extremes in their religion, telling them to say nothing about God but the truth. It then explains who the Messiah is: a messenger of God, a word He placed in Mary, and a spirit from Him. So believe in God and in His messengers, it says, and do not say that there are three; stop, because that is better for you. God is one God, far above having a child, and to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and He is enough as a guardian.

**What the Warning Is About**
The verse is not asking anyone to be careless with his religion; it is telling him not to load it with claims that the truth cannot carry. The sūrah has been correcting one such claim in the verses before it: the slander against Mary (4:156 names it), the boast about the crucifixion (4:157 reports the claim and corrects it), and the statement that God raised him to Himself (4:158 states it). The verse in front of the reader answers the claim that grew out of that history, which is the claim that the Messiah is more than a servant and messenger. The sūrah's list of messengers in the same passage puts Jesus in the line with Noah, Abraham and the others (4:163 names them), which is exactly where the verse leaves him.

**The Three Things the Verse Says About Jesus**
The verse names him the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, then gives three descriptions. He is a messenger of God; he is a word from God placed in Mary, which means he came to be by God's command rather than through the ordinary course; and he is a spirit from Him, a life given by God's command. The Book described the same beginning in another sūrah when it reported the angel's announcement to Mary (66:12 states it), and the same chapter says that nothing about this is hidden from God. The verse then says that believing in God and in His messengers is the way to stop the argument, which is what the chapter has asked of its readers all along: it told them to believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 lists them), it named the men who accept all the messengers and are given their reward (4:152 states it), and it named the men who wanted to choose among them (4:150 describes the position).

**The Command to Stop**
The verse tells the men it addresses to stop, and it gives the reason: it is better for them. The chapter has used the same plain instruction at other points where a wrong idea had taken hold: it told the community not to step over the limits in the matter of marriage and orphans (4:127 answers the question about women, and the chapter's rules on marriage begin at 4:3), it answered the claim about a group's standing carrying them into the garden (4:123 refuses the wish and 4:124 names the condition), and it refused the pick-and-choose attitude to the messengers (4:150) and (4:151 give the position and the verdict). The verse in front of the reader stops the argument at its root: the claim is not a small detail of language, because it puts a creature where the Creator belongs.

**God Is One and Above Having a Child**
The verse states that God is one God, far above having a child, and that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and that He is enough as a guardian. The sūrah has stated the ownership in the same terms several times: it said that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to God and that His knowledge surrounds everything (4:126 states both), that He is the only one who takes care of every affair (4:132 gives that), and that He is able to replace a people with others (4:133 states it). The verse's last phrase about His being enough answers the fear that lies behind the claim: nobody needs a mediator between himself and the One who already owns everything.

**What the Chapter Does With This at Its Close**
The chapter's closing verses carry the same two themes to the end. The address to humanity in the verse before this one tells everyone that the Messenger has come with the truth and that belief is for the believer's own good (4:170 states it), and the closing verses handle the last of the inheritance questions (4:176 gives the rule for a man who leaves neither parent nor child). The sūrah has named the men who follow the light sent down with the Prophet as the successful ones (4:175 states their road), and it has kept the practical duties in view through the whole passage: the guarded prayer of the battle (4:102), the alms and the prayer of the men who are grounded in knowledge (4:162 lists them), the weight of every deed (4:40 sets the scale), and the command to stand for justice even against one's own family (4:135). The verse in front of the reader corrects the last claim that stood between the People of the Book and the message, and it does so with the simplest of words: one God, and a messenger who was a man. The sūrah has told the Prophet to judge by what God showed him (4:105), has named the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116), and has promised the gardens to the men who believe and do good work (4:122). It has recorded the instruction to be mindful of God (4:131), has passed its verdict on the men who wanted a middle way (4:151), and has given the purpose of sending the messengers, which is that no one would have an argument left (4:165). It has said that God bears witness to what was sent down (4:166) and has told the community to stand for the weak who cried out for help (4:75).

---## Verse 4:172

> The Messiah would never be too proud to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels nearest to Allah. Those who are too proud and arrogant to worship Him will be brought before Him all together

**The Messiah Is Not Too Proud to Be a Servant**
The verse says that the Messiah would never consider himself above being a servant of God, and neither would the angels who are closest to Him, and it adds that the men who are too proud and refuse to worship Him will all be brought before Him together. The verse follows the warning to the People of the Book against extremes (4:171), and it answers the claim the verse before it corrected by naming the servant of God as the highest honour there is.

**What the Verse Establishes**
The Book's answer to the elevation of a prophet is not to lower him but to name what he is. The verse puts the Messiah and the nearest angels in one sentence, and it says that neither of them thinks himself above serving God, which means that service is the ground on which the greatest creatures stand. The sūrah has named the Messiah in the same line as the other prophets of the list it gave (4:163 lists Noah, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the rest, and 4:164 names the messengers whose stories were not told), and it named him as a messenger of God, a word placed in Mary, and a spirit from Him (4:171 states the three descriptions). The verse in front of the reader adds the posture that goes with all of it.

**Why the Sūrah Names the Angels**
The verse mentions the angels nearest to God because they are the creatures whose rank nobody disputes, and it makes the point that rank and worship belong together. The chapter had already named the angels in its account of the day of account: it said that the souls of the men who wronged themselves were taken while the angels asked them what they had been doing (4:87 follows the passage on the day when God will gather humanity, and the taking of the souls at death is reported in the same sūrah). It also said that God bears witness and the angels bear witness to what was sent down (4:166 states the witness). The verse in front of the reader takes the highest of the angels and pairs them with the Messiah to show that the creatures closest to God are the first to worship Him.

**The Fate of the Proud**
The verse says that the men who are too proud and refuse to worship will be brought before God all together, and the chapter has warned about pride in several settings: it named the men who kept their meetings at night and thought nobody was watching (the sūrah says nothing in those meetings escaped God), it said that God does not love a man who is arrogant and boastful, and it refused the position of the men who chose which messengers they would accept (4:150 describes their wish and 4:151 gives the verdict). It also named the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 states the answer), and the men who sat with mockers of God's verses (4:140 records the instruction). The verse in front of the reader gathers all of those positions into one picture: the men who would not bow will be brought in front of the One they refused.

**Where the Chapter Stands at This Point**
The verses around this one are the chapter's closing arguments with the People of the Book, and they keep the tone of correction rather than insult. The verse before this one told them not to go to extremes and named the Messiah as a servant and messenger (4:171 gives the warning and the description), and the verse after this one states the reward of the men who believe and do good work and the punishment of the men who are proud (4:173 gives both halves). The sūrah has used the same shape at other points in the chapter: the men who believed and did right were promised their wage while the men who held back were told what their conduct earned (4:162 gives the list of the first), and the men whose belief was a show were told where they end while the door back was opened in the very next verse (4:145 and 4:146 give the two). The chapter had also reminded its readers of the ties that make pride absurd: God created humanity from a single soul (4:1 states it), He owns whatever is in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states it), and the men who knew this best were the ones whose learning showed itself in prayer and giving (4:162 again). The sūrah has named the curse that the being who was promised a share of God's servants brought on himself (4:118 records it), has described the best in religion as the man who hands himself over to God and follows the way of Abraham (4:125), has named the covenant taken from the earlier community (4:154), has named the slander spoken against Mary (4:156), and has named the messengers whose stories were not told to the Prophet (4:164).

---## Verse 4:173

> As for those who believe and do good, He will reward them in full and increase them out of His grace. But those who are too proud and arrogant, He will subject them to a painful punishment. And besides Allah they will find no protector or helper

**Reward for the Believers and Punishment for the Proud**
The verse states the two outcomes that follow the description in the verse before it: the men who believe and do good work will be paid in full and given more out of God's grace, and the men who are too proud to worship will be given a painful punishment and will find no protector or helper besides God. The verse closes the chapter's long argument with the People of the Book and with everyone who thought his standing would carry him.

**The Reward Stated First**
The verse puts the reward first, which is the chapter's habit whenever it sets out the two destinations. The men and women who do good work with faith are told that they will not be wronged by so much as a speck on a date stone (4:124 gives the promise), the men who strive are given ranks and mercy from God (4:96 names both), the men who migrate for God's sake are given room in the earth and a wide provision (4:100 states the promise), and the men who believe and do good work in this chapter are promised gardens under which rivers flow (4:122 names the destination). The verse in front of the reader adds that the reward is not only paid in full but increased, which is the same generosity the sūrah named when it described the men who hold fast to God and are admitted into His mercy (4:175 states it).

**The Punishment and the Pride Behind It**
The punishment is attached to pride, and the chapter has named pride as the reason a person refuses what he knows. It described the men who refused to go out to fight and said their brothers would not have died if they had stayed (the sūrah reports their claim and forbids such talk at 4:72 in its account of the men who stayed behind), the men who were too important to be judged by anyone but their own favourites (4:60 reports the case of the men who wanted a tyrant's court), and the men whose group standing made them sure of the garden (4:123 refuses that wish and 4:124 names the actual condition). The verse in front of the reader gives the proud their sentence, and the next verse turns to address all of humanity with the news that decisive proof has come from their Lord (4:174 states it).

**Nobody to Help**
The verse says that the proud will find no protector and no helper besides God, and the sūrah has used that sentence for the men who trusted in the wrong support. It said that the men who take the other side as allies will find no helper (4:144 gives the instruction and 4:145 names the place), it asked the men who argued a case in this life who would be their advocate on the day (the sūrah puts that question to the men who pleaded for the thief at 4:109), and it told the community that God alone is the guardian who settles every affair (4:45 says that God knows the community's enemies best and is enough as a protector and a helper). The verse in front of the reader names the emptiness of every shelter that is not God, and it names God as the one shelter that remains.

**The Duties the Chapter Has Kept in Front of Its Readers**
The chapter has never left its readers with warnings alone, and the duties it has given run through the same pages: verify what you strike before you strike (4:94 states the rule for the field), stand for justice even when the case cuts against your own family (4:135 sets that standard), treat parents and relatives and neighbours and the traveller well (4:36 gives the list), remember God in every position (4:103 gives the instruction), and keep your agreements (4:172's passage names the servants and 4:129 handles the marriage that is left hanging). The sūrah has also named the men who were given knowledge and faith, whose learning does not stop them from praying and giving (4:162 lists the conditions), and it has warned the community against the wish of the men who follow their own appetites (4:27 names the wish, and 4:40 sets the exact scale of every deed). The verse in front of the reader is the last of the chapter's verdicts before the call to all humanity, and it holds the same balance the sūrah has kept from the beginning: reward for the men who do the work, and no shelter for the men who think they do not need to. The sūrah has described the knowledge given to the Prophet for the arguments brought to him (4:113), has named the false names the idolaters call on (4:117), has named the promises the lying being made to them (4:119), has handled the wife who must not be left hanging (4:129), and has placed both rewards with God (4:134). It has described the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139), has named the men who block others from the road of God (4:167), and has corrected the claim that the Messiah was more than a servant (4:171). It has said that no deed escapes the exact account (4:40) and has told the community to stand for the weak who cried out for help (4:75).

---## Verse 4:174

> O humanity! There has come to you conclusive evidence from your Lord. And We have sent down to you a brilliant light

**Clear Proof and a Bright Light**
The verse addresses all humanity with the news that decisive proof has come from their Lord and that a clear light has been sent down. The verse follows the two verdicts of the verse before it (4:173) and it opens the last movement of the chapter before the final inheritance rule.

**What the Proof Is**
The Book calls the message itself the proof, which is the same claim the passage has been making against the men who asked for something else: they asked for a written revelation brought down from the sky (4:153 reports the demand), and they argued about the claims of their own history (4:154 names the covenant and the mountain lifted over them). The sūrah has answered all of it by naming the messenger and the book, and the same chapter had already said that the Prophets came with good news and warnings so that no one would be left with an argument after them (4:165 states that purpose). The sūrah also said that God bears witness to what He sent down (4:166 states it), which leaves the reader with the proof and its witness.

**The Light the Verse Names**
The light is the guidance the book gives to the person who reads it, and the chapter has described what that light does. It said that God guides by it to the ways of peace and brings people out of darkness by His permission, which is stated in another sūrah, and the chapter in front of the reader named the men who follow the light sent down with the Prophet as the successful ones (4:175 states their road). It said that God's will in the book is to make matters clear and to guide the reader to the paths of the men who came before (4:26 states the will), and it named the men who were given knowledge and faith as the ones who understand what was sent (4:162 lists them). The verse in front of the reader tells the reader that the light is not hidden or private: it has been sent to him.

**What the Chapter Has Asked of the Reader**
The chapter has been asking the same thing from its opening pages, and the call in this verse is the plainest form of it. The sūrah began by addressing humanity through the One who created them from a single soul (4:1 states it), and it went on to name every group in the community it was addressing: the men whose belief was a show (4:142 describes their prayer), the men who waited to see which side won (4:141 states their habit), the men who blocked others from the road (4:167 gives the charge), and the men who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 states the answer). Against all of them it named the men who did the work: the men who migrate for God's sake (4:100), the men whose knowledge shows in prayer and giving (4:162), the men who turn back and hold fast to God (4:146), and the men and women who do good work with faith (4:124). The verse in front of the reader calls everyone to the proof that has already arrived, and it tells the reader what he is being asked to do with it.

**Where the Light Leads**
The verses after this one name the destination of the men who take the light: God will admit the men who believe in Him and hold fast to Him into His mercy and grace and guide them to Himself along a straight path (4:175 states all of it). The chapter then closes with the ruling for the man who dies leaving neither parent nor child (4:176 gives the case). The sūrah has kept the same two ideas together all the way through, and it stated them in the middle of the chapter when it said that God does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom (4:40 uses the speck on a date stone). It also warned about the wish of the men who follow their own appetites (4:27 names it) and about the marriage that is treated lightly (4:28 speaks of the burden God lightens, and 4:29 forbids taking property by false means). Its instruction to the weak and the helpless was stated plainly when it told the community to stand for the men, women and children who cried out for help (4:75 gives the command, and 4:99 describes the helpless who are excused). The verse in front of the reader gathers the whole chapter into two words, proof and light, and the reader is told what to do with both. The sūrah has given the community the prayer in every situation it could face (4:103 gives the instruction), has told the Prophet to judge by what God showed him (4:105), and has described the knowledge he was given (4:113). It has praised the private talk that urges giving and reconciliation (4:114), has named the wrong that cannot be forgiven (4:116), has named the promises the lying being made to the idolaters (4:120), and has promised the gardens to the men who believe and do good work (4:122). It has said that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God with the knowledge that surrounds it (4:126), has handled the couple whose marriage had gone cold (4:128), has said that a people can be replaced (4:133), and has listed the prophets who carried the same message before the Prophet (4:163). It has addressed all humanity with the news that the Messenger has come with the truth (4:170), has corrected the claim about the Messiah (4:171), and has named the helpless who are excused from the journey (4:99).

---## Verse 4:175
> As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him, He will admit them into His mercy and grace and guide them to Himself through the Straight Path

**Those Who Hold Fast to God**
The verse names the men and women who believe in God and hold fast to Him, and it promises them three things. God will admit them into His mercy and grace, and He will guide them to Himself along a straight path. The verse follows the call to humanity with the proof and the light (4:174 gives both), and it describes the people who take hold of what has been sent.

**What Holding Fast Means**
The phrase describes a person who has taken hold of something and will not let go. The chapter used it earlier for the people who came out of hypocrisy: those who turned from what they were doing, set their conduct right, held firmly to God and made their devotion sincere, who are counted with the believers (4:146 gives the four conditions). The same sūrah told the community to obey God, the Messenger and those in authority among them, and to take any disagreement back to God and the Messenger. What this verse describes is the posture the whole chapter has been asking for: not a claim about belonging to a group, but a grip on the message.

**The Mercy and the Grace**
The mercy and grace promised here are the same pair the sūrah used earlier, where it said that the men and women who do good work with faith will enter the gardens and be wronged by no more than the speck on a date stone (4:124 states it). It also promised those who migrate for God's sake that they will find room in the earth and plenty (4:100 gives the promise). And it named those who believe in what was sent down to the Prophet and in what was sent before him, who keep the prayer and pay the alms, as the ones who will be given their wage (4:162 lists them). What a person receives for holding fast, then, is forgiveness he did not earn and generosity that is not counted.

**The Straight Path**
The verse ends by naming the straight path, the road the whole chapter has been describing since its opening pages. The sūrah names the people who walk it: those who believe in God, His Messenger, the Book given to him and the Books given before (4:136 lists the four), those who ask forgiveness after doing wrong (4:110 opens the door), those whose devotion to God is sincere (4:146 names that condition), and those who were given knowledge and faith (4:162 appears again). The road is not a puzzle. Those who take hold of God are placed on it.

**What the Chapter Keeps Around This Promise**
The chapter closes with this promise and with one more practical ruling. The verse before it addresses all humanity with the proof and the light (4:174 states both), and the verse after it gives the inheritance ruling for a man who leaves neither parent nor child (4:176 gives the ruling). The sūrah keeps the same two subjects together through its closing pages, the call to believe and the rules for ordinary life. It gave the community the prayer in every situation it could face (4:103 gives the instruction), and it named the payment owed by a man who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 states it). It names the helpless who are excused from the journey (4:99 states their case) and the people of the earlier community who believed and did right (4:174 names the ones called and 4:163 lists the prophets who carried the message). It also states the principle that the call is for the reader's own good and not for God's benefit (4:147 asks what God would gain by punishing a grateful believer).

This verse brings the chapter's account of belief to its plainest form, and the last verse of the chapter returns to the law that governs a family after a death. The sūrah has also described those who walked away from the road once it had been made clear to them (4:115 states their case) and those who looked for honour in the wrong company (4:139 gives the answer), so that the reader can see the difference between holding fast and letting go. Its instruction not to waste what a person has been given stands in the same sūrah, and those who hold fast are named as people whose hearts were kept steady (4:26 speaks of the will to make matters clear and to guide). The sūrah tells the Prophet to judge by what God has shown him (4:105 gives the instruction), promises the gardens to those who believe and do good work (4:122 gives the promise), and places both rewards with God (4:134 states it). It lists the prophets who carried the message before the Prophet (4:163 lists them), names the messengers whose stories were not told (4:164 names them), corrects the claim about the Messiah (4:171 corrects it), describes the servants who are not too proud to worship (4:172 describes them) and states the two outcomes for the believers and the proud (4:173 states them). It also names the payment owed by the man who kills a believer by mistake (4:92 states it).
verses.176:
> They ask you ˹for a ruling, O Prophet˺. Say, “Allah gives you a ruling regarding those who die without children or parents.” If a man dies childless and leaves behind a sister, she will inherit one-half of his estate, whereas her brother will inherit all of her estate if she dies childless. If this person leaves behind two sisters, they together will inherit two-thirds of the estate. But if the deceased leaves male and female siblings, a male’s share will be equal to that of two females. Allah makes ˹this˺ clear to you so you do not go astray. And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of all things

**The Last Ruling on Inheritance**
The verse answers a question put to the Prophet about the man who dies leaving neither parent nor child, and it sets out the shares: if a man dies childless and leaves a sister, she takes half of his estate; and if she dies childless and leaves a brother, he takes all of it. Then it gives the case of two sisters, who take two thirds between them, and of brothers and sisters together, where the man takes the share of two women. The verse closes by saying that God makes the matter clear so that the community will not go astray, and that He knows all things.

**Why the Chapter Ends With This**
The chapter opened with the rules of inheritance for children, parents and spouses, and it gave them with a warning attached: the men and women who obey are admitted to gardens and the men and women who disobey are punished (4:11 and 4:12 give the shares, and 4:13 and 4:14 give the two destinations). Then it dealt with the inheritance of the widow and the orphan whose rights were being swallowed (4:10 names the fire for those who consume the property of orphans, and 4:7 states the shares due to men and women alike). The sūrah returns to the same subject at its close because the community kept asking about the cases the earlier rules had not settled, and this verse answers the last of them.

**What the Kalālah Case Is**
The case in this verse is called the inheritance of a person who leaves neither a parent nor a child, and the ruling covers the brothers and sisters of the dead person. The verse gives three arrangements: one sister alone takes half of the estate; two sisters share two thirds; and when brothers and sisters inherit together, each brother takes twice the share of each sister. The rule is the same principle that runs through the chapter's earlier shares for sons and daughters, and the Book states here the reason it gives for all of it: God makes His ruling plain so that the community will not wander.

**How the Rule Works With the Earlier Ones**
The sūrah had already set the shares for the closest relatives and told the community what to do with a will and with debts (4:11 and 4:12 set the shares, and 4:12 speaks of what is left after a will and debts are settled). It also answered the community's question about women and orphans and told the community to give the orphan his property and not to trade the good for the bad (4:127 deals with the question and the chapter's earlier verses forbid consuming what belongs to the weak). The sūrah keeps the whole set of rules together by giving them the same closing sentence: whoever obeys God and His Messenger is admitted to gardens, and the men who overstep the limits that have been set are punished (4:13 and 4:14 give both sides). The verse in front of the reader ends the chapter on the same note of exactness with which it began, and it is the last of the chapter's answers about the family.

**What the Chapter Leaves With the Reader**
The chapter has moved from the rules of the family to the rules of the community and back again, and it has kept the same frame around everything. It told the community to return what was placed in its trust and to judge fairly (4:58 gives both), it told the believers to stand for justice even when the case cuts against their own family (4:135 sets the standard), it named the men who were forbidden their own property by the way the community treated them (the chapter's rules about women and the weak appear at the verses on the family), and it named the men who traded the rights of the weak for their own advantage (4:160 records the charges against the earlier community and 4:161 names the interest they took). The sūrah's last words are the same as its method throughout: God states the law plainly, and He knows every case. The verse before the reader follows the call to humanity with the proof and the light (4:174 states both) and the promise to the men who hold fast to God (4:175 states the three gifts), so that the chapter closes with the law and the light together. The sūrah also reminded its readers along the way that God's knowledge surrounds everything in the heavens and the earth (4:126 states that) and that no deed escapes the account (4:40 sets the scale). The chapter's final sentence leaves the reader with a law that names every case it was asked about and with the assurance that the One who gave it knows the cases nobody has asked about yet. The sūrah had named the destination of the men who overstep the limits God set for the family (4:14 states it), had stated the shares due to men and women alike in the middle of its rules (4:7 names them), and had closed its account of the earlier community with the charges against it (4:160 names the foods that were forbidden and 4:174's own passage calls humanity to the proof). The chapter also said that God's will in this book is to make matters clear (4:26 states the will).
